newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechens reveal might at presidential inauguration.
newsitem.headline: Chechens reveal might at presidential inauguration.

text.p: If Russia needed any reminding why it failed to crush Chechen separatism, it was here in the breakaway region's capital Grozny on Wednesday at the inauguration ceremony of its first post-war president.
Hundreds of armed men swarmed around the pink, neo-classical suburban building where Chechnya's new president was sworn in for want of a better place in a city wrecked by 21 months of fighting.
Many wore military fatigues, some civilian clothes, a couple of them had even teamed dark suits with their automatic rifles, but all had the hardened look of battle.

In a short, dignified ceremony, the top field commanders whom president-elect Aslan Maskhadov led against Russia lined up on stage alongside Maskhadov while their underlings trained their guns on the assembled audience just in case.

For almost two years these men had hidden from the Russian troops sent to flush them out -- in ruined buildings, in the forested slopes of the Caucasus mountains or by simply posing as unarmed civilians until it was time to strike.
"I tore apart four contract soldiers with this," said Aslan Baysarov with a smile, flicking open a long knife under this correspondent's nose.

Outside on the street, after the white-haired Maskhadov, a former Soviet colonel, had sworn an oath in front of the commanders of the rebel force, the men let loose with their weapons in a triumphant show of force.
Mothers in the crowd covered their children's ears but otherwise did not even flinch at the sound of hundreds of automatic rifles being fired into the air.
Some of the men even let off grenade launchers as bullet casings rained down on the crowd from the bright blue sky.
But the rebels, who fought in loose groups joined by other members of the Moslem population when their homes were threatened by the Russian advance, were generally in peaceful mood.
"We don't intend to fight any more," said Ali Amagayev, lounging around after the ceremony with a group of friends.
Asked what they planned to do now that the war was over he said they all had different plans. "Some will go to their collective farms, some into commerce, others will stay in the military," he said.

The rebel leaders began to go their separate ways after Maskhadov signed a peace deal with Russia in August paving the way for the withdrawal of the troops in return for a postponement of the issue of Chechnya's status.

Several of them stood against him in last month's election but they came together for the ceremony, defying, at least temporarily, predictions by some Russian politicians that the withdrawal of troops from Chechnya would lead to civil war.
Outgoing President Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, who plans to go into political opposition and accused Maskhadov of compromising on independence, gave a speech welcoming his election.

But then he left, saying: "There are people here I cannot sit with." He did not make clear whether he meant his fellow Chechens or representatives in the audience from Russia, which still insists Chechnya must not split away.
Hardline rebel commander Shamil Basayev, who also stood against Maskhadov for the presidency, took a gentler line.
"I am very glad that we could carry out this inauguration together so that, just as we fought this war with honour, so with honour we can move to live peacefully on the path to freedom," he said.

The bearded Basayev, who had donned a three-piece suit and silk cravat for the occasion, was declared a terrorist by Moscow after he raided a Russian town and took hundreds of people hostage in a hospital in June 1995.

He is one of the rebels excluded from an amnesty for combatants in Chechnya currently being prepared by the Russian parliament. But after its military humiliation at the hands of the rebels, Moscow is in no mood to try to arrest him.
